content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to introduce any numeric figures that weren't explicitly labeled—using placeholders like {alert_raised}, {began}, {duration} instead of writing out specific times or durations, and avoiding spelled-out numbers like "six hours" in favor of vaguer phrasing like "the preceding several hours."

Looking at the causal chain, the symptom is just that an error-rate alert fired without any corresponding service degradation visible in the metrics. The chain shows the alert fired, metrics stayed within baseline during the window, and then stops there since the reason the rule fired remains undetermined—I can't rule out a real fault since none of the metrics I read actually came from while the service might have been broken, and the window examined ended right around the alert's onset.

That timing gap matters: the alert fired at 14:59:15 but metrics are anchored to 14:59, so the alert minute itself likely isn't captured in the data I reviewed. I'm noting this as a contributing factor since the investigation concluded quickly from data that stopped right at the alert minute. For action items, I'll propose recording the rule's evaluated value and triggering series going forward, re-checking once metrics for the alert minute become available before closing this as disproven, and reviewing the alert threshold itself.

action_items.item: Before Argus closes an incident as DISPROVEN, have it re-read the service's metrics after the alert time has been ingested, so the verdict rests on data that covers the alert period. If that data is still missing, flag the verdict as unconfirmed.
Attach the rule's evaluated value, threshold, and source series to each HighErrorRate alert so the investigator can compare the rule's input with the service's metrics.
Have the owner of the io-shop HighErrorRate rule review its query, threshold and evaluation window, and any gaps in its data source, to find out why it fired without a matching service fault.

causal_chain.step: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was raised at {alert_raised} and Argus took it up as an incident. No user-facing failure was observed or measured. The only evidence of a problem is the alert itself.

Argus's investigator read the service's per-minute metrics ending at the alert minute. No minute in the window departed from baseline in error rate, latency percentiles, memory use or the rule's own reading.
Because nothing in the window matched the alarm's claim of an error rate above threshold, Argus concluded that the rule fired rather than the service failing, and moved the incident to DISPROVEN.
The record does not say why the rule fired. The metrics read show no input that would have tripped it, and none were read from while the alert was active. The chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: No metrics from while the alert was active were available to the investigation. The window ended at the alert minute, so the incident was closed as disproven without data from the period the alert describes. A real but brief or late-onset fault cannot be excluded.
The alert does not record what value it evaluated or which series crossed the threshold. The investigator therefore could not tell why the rule fired when the service metrics looked normal.
The rule's behaviour was not reviewed after it fired without a service fault. If it is misconfigured or reads a faulty series, it will page again with nothing to find.

input.executive_summary: An automated alert said the io-shop service had a high error rate. Argus, the automated incident responder, looked at the service's recent metrics. Over the several hours before the alert they showed nothing unusual. Argus closed the incident as disproven, meaning the alert fired without a matching failure in the data. No user impact was measured. The record also holds no metrics from after the alert fired, so the service's state during and after the alert is unknown. Argus's response took only a few seconds, and that is a measure of the response, not of the service. No fix was applied because no fault was found. Why the alert fired is still unexplained.

got_lucky: If the alert was real and began just as it fired, the closure would have hidden a live outage. Nothing in the record shows that happened, but nothing rules it out.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert and reached a clear verdict within seconds.
The investigator checked a wide set of series, including the rule's own reading, rather than only the error rate.
The investigator said plainly that no cause was determined instead of inventing one.
went_wrong: The verdict was reached with no metrics from while the alert was active, so DISPROVEN is weaker than it sounds.
The record cannot explain why the rule fired, and the alert carries too little detail to find out.
No action items existed beforehand to help follow up a rule that fires without a fault.

input.root_cause: The HighErrorRate rule on io-shop fired, but no metric Argus read, including error rate, latency, memory and the rule's own reading, departed from baseline over the preceding hours. The record does not show why the rule fired. Argus could not read metrics from the period the alert covers, so it could not confirm or rule out a real fault.
input.symptom: Error-rate alert fired, but no service failure was found
